title: Limited-memory convex optimization
formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors, the deterministic first-order oracle complexity \(T(d,M,\varepsilon)\) of minimizing a globally convex, Euclidean \(1\)-Lipschitz function with a global minimizer in the unit ball, when only \(M\) bits can be retained between queries. The target is the entire tradeoff for integers \(d\geq1\), \(M\geq0\) and real \(0<\varepsilon\leq1/4\), including the parameters for which \(T(d,M,\varepsilon)=\infty\).
why: The tradeoff separates acquiring information about a convex objective from retaining that information for later decisions. A full answer would quantify when nearly linear storage can preserve fast convergence and when the geometry needed for a small number of queries forces substantially larger memory.
status_note: The full tradeoff is open in the 2019 source. A review on 13 September 2026 found substantial later endpoint and partial-tradeoff results, but no complete characterization in the precise source model. The bounded later-work check is not an exhaustive certification of current openness.

progress.text: Woodworth and Srebro define the finite-state oracle model and ask for its full minimax tradeoff.
Blanchard, Zhang and Jaillet prove a nearly quadratic memory barrier at the optimal-query endpoint for unit-ball optimization.
Recursive cutting-plane algorithms give additional upper bounds, particularly at very high accuracy.
Menart, Nikolov and Shamir post stronger lower bounds in the bounded-query optimization model; these do not themselves characterize the full function on this card.

importance.reason: A fundamental tradeoff between two distinct resources in first-order optimization, with major endpoint lower bounds and substantial unresolved parameter ranges.

sentences: First-order convex optimization learns about an objective through queries returning its value and a subgradient.
The source asks how the number of queries needed for a prescribed accuracy changes when the algorithm has limited working memory.
It highlights methods with strong oracle complexity whose stored geometric information can require quadratic space in dimension.
The question is whether that memory cost is inherent or can be traded away without losing the optimal query rate.
A sharp tradeoff would distinguish information acquired from the oracle from information that must remain available between optimization steps.

definitions: Let \(\mathcal F_d\) contain all convex functions \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) such that \(|f(x)-f(y)|\leq\|x-y\|_2\) for every \(x,y\), and such that some global minimizer \(x_*\) satisfies \(\|x_*\|_2\leq1\). A subgradient at \(x\) is a vector \(g\) with \(f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle\) for every \(y\in\mathbb R^d\). A query at any \(x\in\mathbb R^d\) returns the exact pair \((f(x),g)\) for any valid subgradient; correctness is required for every sequence of such choices. An \(M\)-bit, \(t\)-query algorithm consists of deterministic maps \(\phi_i:\{0,1\}^M\to\mathbb R^d\), \(\psi_i:\{0,1\}^M\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d\to\{0,1\}^M\) for \(1\leq i\leq t\), and \(\zeta:\{0,1\}^M\to\mathbb R^d\). Starting with \(s_0=0^M\), it queries \(x_i=\phi_i(s_{i-1})\), receives \((f(x_i),g_i)\), and sets \(s_i=\psi_i(s_{i-1},f(x_i),g_i)\). Its final output is \(\zeta(s_t)\); for \(t=0\) it is \(\zeta(s_0)\). All maps may depend on \(d,M,t,\varepsilon\), but not on the unknown function. They are unrestricted mathematical maps: computing an update can use arbitrary real operations and temporary memory. Only the retained state is limited; there is no runtime, uniformity or computability requirement on these maps. The iteration index is implicit in the maps and is not charged to memory. Define \(R(d,M,t)=\inf_A\sup_{f\in\mathcal F_d,\,(g_i)}[f(\zeta(s_t))-\min_x f(x)]\), and \(T(d,M,\varepsilon)=\min\{t\in\mathbb N_0:R(d,M,t)\leq\varepsilon\}\), with the minimum of the empty set equal to infinity. The infimum over algorithms need not be attained: \(R\leq\varepsilon\) means that for every \(\eta>0\) some algorithm has worst-case error at most \(\varepsilon+\eta\). Queries and outputs are not restricted to the unit ball.
answer_criterion: Supply a noncircular characterization \(G(d,M,\varepsilon)\in[0,\infty]\) and a complete Lean-checked proof of \(cG\leq T\leq CG\) throughout the stated domain, for fixed \(c,C>0\). Prove exactly which parameters have infinite complexity. The memory argument and requested accuracy must be those stated, without an unstated constant enlargement of memory or accuracy. Upper bounds must respect the infimum convention. Resolving only optimal-query memory requirements or one accuracy regime is not a characterization of the full tradeoff.

context_blocks.text: This is Question 1 of Woodworth and Srebro’s 2019 contribution, with its preferred constant-factor accuracy selected explicitly. The source also permits a weaker polylogarithmic characterization and poses several subsidiary endpoint questions; those alternatives are not the acceptance criterion here.

The normalization loses no scale parameter: a Lipschitz constant \(L>0\) and a known minimizer radius \(B>0\) replace the accuracy by \(\varepsilon/(LB)\). The formal target retains the source’s global-function model and its bottleneck-memory convention, rather than total machine space.

The source exhibits gradient descent with \(O(\varepsilon^{-2})\) queries and \(O(d\log(1/\varepsilon))\) retained bits, and a discretized center-of-mass method with \(O(d\log(1/\varepsilon))\) queries and \(O(d^2\log^2(1/\varepsilon))\) bits. These are achievable resource pairs; neither states the optimal query rate in every dimension and accuracy regime.

Blanchard, Zhang and Jaillet’s 2023 work establishes a nearly quadratic memory barrier for optimal query complexity in convex minimization over the unit ball. This addresses a source endpoint question, not the complete three-parameter tradeoff. Their separate recursive cutting-plane work gives additional memory-query upper bounds, including a high-accuracy regime.

Menart, Nikolov and Shamir’s July 2026 preprint strengthens deterministic and randomized lower bounds and reports a sharp transition near quadratic memory. Its stated model restricts queries to the feasible unit ball. No transfer of its numerical bounds to the global, unrestricted-query model above is assumed by this card.

A real-valued oracle answer can carry unlimited precision, but retaining it requires encoding it in the next finite state. Conversely, restricting temporary arithmetic would create a different problem. These distinctions are central to what a memory lower bound establishes.
